Title: Telnet is open
Description: Telnet sends usernames, passwords and everything typed in plain text. Anyone on the network path can read them. Telnet on routers, switches and IoT devices is also a common target for botnets.
Evidence: TCP 23 accepted a connection; banner: Microsoft Windows XP telnetd
Remediation: Disable the Telnet service on the device and use SSH instead. | Windows: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName TelnetServer (older systems). | Network gear (e.g. Cisco): 'line vty 0 15' → 'transport input ssh'. | If Telnet can't be disabled, restrict it to a management VLAN with firewall rules.

Title: SMB signing is not required
StatusNote: Sample: accepted until the device is replaced in Q1.
Description: Without mandatory SMB signing, an attacker on the local network can relay or tamper with file-sharing traffic (NTLM relay attacks). Domain controllers require signing by default; other servers often don't.
Evidence: SMB2 NEGOTIATE response SecurityMode: signing enabled, not required (dialect ?).
Remediation: Group Policy › Computer Configuration › Windows Settings › Security Settings › Local Policies › Security Options: |   "Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)" = Enabled. | Or per server (admin PowerShell): Set-SmbServerConfiguration -RequireSecuritySignature $true -Force | Samba: set 'server signing = mandatory' in smb.conf. | Run gpupdate /force, then rescan.

Title: SMBv1 is enabled
Description: The server still accepts SMB version 1, a 30-year-old file-sharing protocol with serious design flaws. Worms and ransomware such as WannaCry and NotPetya spread through SMBv1. Modern Windows, macOS and Linux clients don't need it.
Evidence: SMB1 NEGOTIATE offering only "NT LM 0.12" was accepted by the server.
Remediation: Windows Server/PC (admin PowerShell): Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false -Force | Remove the feature completely: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol (restart required). | Across a domain: Group Policy › Computer Configuration › Administrative Templates › MS Security Guide › Configure SMBv1 server = Disabled. | NAS / Samba devices: set the minimum SMB protocol to SMB2 (Samba: 'server min protocol = SMB2_10'). | Rescan this host to confirm the finding is resolved.

Title: TLS 1.0 enabled
Description: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 were formally retired in 2021 (RFC 8996). They rely on weak hashing and are no longer accepted by modern browsers.
Evidence: Server accepted ClientHello for: TLS 1.0. Supported overall: TLS 1.0, TLS 1.2.
Remediation: Allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. | Windows/IIS/RDP: disable old protocols and ciphers under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL, or use IIS Crypto / a hardening GPO, then restart. | Apache: SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3 and SSLCipherSuite with modern AEAD suites. | nginx: ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_ciphers with ECDHE+AESGCM/CHACHA20 suites. | Appliances and printers: set the minimum TLS version in the device's web admin, and update its firmware if the option is missing. | Rescan to confirm.

Title: Weak TLS cipher suites accepted (RC4/3DES/DES)
Description: The server accepts outdated ciphers. RC4 has known biases and 3DES is vulnerable to the SWEET32 birthday attack.
Remediation: Allow only AEAD suites with forward secrecy (ECDHE with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). | Windows/IIS/RDP: disable old protocols and ciphers under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL, or use IIS Crypto / a hardening GPO, then restart. | Apache: SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3 and SSLCipherSuite with modern AEAD suites. | nginx: ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_ciphers with ECDHE+AESGCM/CHACHA20 suites. | Appliances and printers: set the minimum TLS version in the device's web admin, and update its firmware if the option is missing.
